title: Eye of the Serpent
caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 2835, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, J. Lee, and the PHANGS-HST TeamAcknowledgement: Judy Schmidt (Geckzilla)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The twisting pattern of NGC 2835's many spiral arms creates the illusion of an eye. Fittingly, this barred spiral lies near the head of Hydra, the water snake, a southern constellation. It is just over half as wide as the Milky Way.

Bright blue areas in its outer spiral arms show where near-ultraviolet light is being given off more strongly, a sign of recent or ongoing star formation. A supermassive black hole, millions of times the mass of the Sun, is known to sit at the galaxy's center, though it cannot be seen here.

Hubble imaged NGC 2835 for PHANGS-HST, a large survey that studies the links between cold gas and young stars in many nearby galaxies. In this galaxy, cold, dense gas gives rise to large numbers of young stars in big star-forming regions.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, combining five filters from 275 to 814 nm, spanning ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light. The colors assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: Ultraviolet and near-infrared light are invisible to the eye, and the blue star-forming regions stand out partly because of that ultraviolet data.

explore: The survey expects to capture more than 100 000 star-forming regions and gas clouds in other galaxies, and aims to clarify how cold gas, star formation and a galaxy's overall shape are connected. It is part of the wider PHANGS program, working with ALMA and the MUSE instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope.
alt: A barred spiral galaxy with multiple twisting arms dotted with bright blue regions, resembling an eye.
